extracted.intended_audience: judges and lawyers handling patent infringement trials (federal court juries)
extracted.subtask_short: patent jury instructions for infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for adjudicating patent infringement, invalidity, willfulness, and damages issues in federal-court patent trials. Provides definitions, burdens of proof, claim-construction guidance, infringement/invalidity doctrines, and damages frameworks for juries and trial judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a patent is and how one is obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid United States patent gives the patent holder exclusive rights (e.g., to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the invention) for a statutory term. To obtain a patent one files an application with the PTO including a specification and claims; the PTO examiner reviews prior art and issues office actions; the prosecution history records communications between applicant and examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the specification must describe what the invention is, how it works, and how to make and use it so others skilled in the field can do so; claims define the boundaries of protection; PTO allowance is not dispositive of validity because the court can find a claim invalid based on evidence not before the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of the patent document (cover page, abstract, drawings, specification, claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent document includes a cover page (grant date, patent number, inventor, filing date, cited references), an abstract, drawings illustrating the invention, a written description (specification), and numbered patent claims at the end that define the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court/jury may be directed to these parts to understand the asserted patent; the specification includes the 'best way' believed by the inventor at filing and supports claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's role in claim construction (meaning of claim terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge determines the correct construction or meaning of words in the patent claims; jurors must accept and apply those meanings in deciding infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction to read and apply the words as the court has interpreted them; court may provide a glossary of patent and technical terms and add technical terms expected at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party has the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence, the evidence must persuade the jury that the claim or defense is more probable than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for many affirmative issues (e.g., infringement, entitlement to damages). Committee adopted 'more probable than not' as the phrase; jury should base decision on all evidence regardless of who presented it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the burden is clear and convincing evidence, the evidence must persuade the jury that the claim or defense is highly probable — an intermediate standard higher than preponderance but lower than beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically applies to invalidity defenses; jury should base decision on all the evidence. Committee adopted 'highly probable' as the phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art generally includes things that existed before the claimed invention and were publicly known or used in a publicly accessible way in the country, or were patented or described in a publication in any country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner reviews prior art when prosecuting the application; the court will give a specific legal definition of prior art relevant to invalidity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (literal) infringement — element-by-element comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove direct literal infringement the patent holder must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product or method includes every requirement (element/step) of the asserted claim as the court has interpreted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any requirement/step recited in the claim is omitted in the accused product/method, there is no literal infringement. No intent or knowledge is required for literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended 'comprising' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' means 'including' or 'containing but not limited to' — a claim using 'comprising' is infringed if the accused product/method includes all recited requirements, even if it has additional items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a table 'comprising' tabletop, legs, glue is infringed by a table that also has wheels. Cites authorities that 'comprised of' has same open-ended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Consisting essentially of' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting essentially of' means the claimed invention may include additional unlisted requirements provided those additions do not materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention as defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims with this language are infringed only if added elements do not materially affect the basic and novel features of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Consisting of' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting of' means the claimed invention contains only what is expressly stated in the claim (except it does not limit aspects unrelated to the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product/method infringes only if it includes all stated requirements and does not include additional requirements unless those are unrelated to the invention. Impurities ordinarily associated with a listed requirement do not necessarily avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim includes all requirements of the independent claim it refers to plus additional requirements; infringement of a dependent claim must be determined separately even if the independent claim is infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the independent claim is not infringed, the dependent claim cannot be infringed; if independent is infringed, jury still must assess whether dependent's additional requirements are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the doctrine of equivalents a claim requirement is present in an accused product/method if the difference between the claim requirement and the corresponding aspect of the accused product/method is insubstantial (i.e., identical or equivalent on a requirement-by-requirement basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the accused structure/step performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result (function-way-result test), and whether persons of ordinary skill believed the two were interchangeable at the time of infringement; equivalence is evaluated at time of infringement; prosecution history estoppel and other limitations may bar some equivalents and are for the judge to resolve when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'means' (or step) claim element recites a means for performing a function rather than a structure; such claim elements cover the structure, material, or acts described in the specification for performing that function, and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove literal infringement of a means-plus-function element the patent holder must show (1) the accused device employs a structure/act identical or equivalent to the structure disclosed in the specification, and (2) that the structure in the accused device performs the identical function specified in the claim. Equivalence under §112 ¶6 requires insubstantial differences and is evaluated as of issuance; §112 ¶6 equivalence is not necessarily coextensive with doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — overview (inducing and contributory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement takes two forms: inducing infringement (encouraging or urging another to infringe) and contributory infringement (supplying components used in a patented invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect infringement requires a finding of direct infringement by another for each instance of indirect infringement; statutory bases are 35 U.S.C. §§271(b) and (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing infringement — elements and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inducement the patent holder must show by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the alleged inducer actively encouraged or instructed another to use a product or perform a process in a way that infringes the patent claims; (2) the alleged inducer knew of the patent; (3) the alleged inducer knew or should have known that the encouragement would induce infringement; and (4) another person actually infringed the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent holder must prove specific intent to induce infringement — knowing inducement of infringement, not merely knowing the acts that constitute infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement occurs when a party with knowledge of the patent supplies a component for use in a patented product or process and (1) the component is a material part of the invention; (2) the component is especially made or adapted for use in an infringing way and the supplier knows of that use; and (3) the component has no substantial non-infringing uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the component is a staple or commodity with substantial noninfringing uses, providing it is not contributory infringement. Contributory infringement requires proof of direct infringement by another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful infringement may be found if the patent holder proves by clear and convincing evidence (or as instructed in a case-by-case manner) that the alleged infringer acted with reckless disregard of whether the claim was infringed or was invalid or unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury's willfulness finding should not directly affect the damage award; judge will take willfulness into account for enhanced damages under governing law. Model verdict asks whether willfulness is 'highly probable' (clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim must be supported by an adequate written description in the specification that shows the inventor possessed the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity on written-description grounds must be proven by clear and convincing evidence; model verdict includes written-description question framed as 'highly probable' invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim must be enabled by a description sufficiently full and clear to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement invalidity is to be proven by clear and convincing evidence; jury considers the level of ordinary skill and the sufficiency of the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of filing the patent application, the inventor must have disclosed the best mode contemplated for carrying out the invention; failure to disclose a genuine best mode may render the patent invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best-mode invalidity is a question for the factfinder and must be proven by clear and convincing evidence; the specification should disclose what the inventor believed to be the best way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — public use, prior publication, prior invention by others
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated (not new) if a single prior art reference or prior use/disclosure (in this country or published elsewhere) discloses all elements of the claim; anticipation can include public use, known use, or prior publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation must be proven by clear and convincing evidence; separate instructions address 'publicly used or known, or previously published' anticipation and anticipation by prior invention by someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars and timing (notice/marking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutory bars can prevent patentability based on dates of public disclosure or activity. For damages, a patent holder must give actual or constructive notice (marking) to recover damages — damages generally run from the date actual or constructive notice was given (or for method claims, from issuance or when infringement began).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. §287 and case law cited; jury should not award damages for infringement occurring before notice/marking, except for method claims where damages begin at issuance or when infringement began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (nonobviousness) — general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid as obvious if, considering the scope and content of the prior art, differences over the prior art, and the level of ordinary skill in the art, the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is typically proved by clear and convincing evidence; the instructions include breakdowns (scope/content of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill) and alternative formulations. Jury should consider objective indicia where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art / differences over prior art / level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess obviousness jurors must (1) determine the scope and content of the prior art, (2) identify differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, and (3) determine the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual inquiries feed into the legal conclusion of obviousness; evidence may include expert testimony, prior references, and industry practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general burden and calculation framework
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jury finds infringement and not invalidity, it must decide money damages to compensate the patent holder. The patent holder bears the burden of proving damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages questions include when damages begin (notice/marking), lost profits, and reasonable royalty; jury should not award damages for infringement before notice unless method claims (special rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — when damages begin (marking/notice rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages run from the date the accused infringer received actual or constructive notice (whichever was first). For method claims, the notice requirement does not apply; damages for method claims begin on the date the patent issued or the date infringement began, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. §287 and cases; jury should not award pre-notice damages for product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Panduit factors (four elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits the patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence: (1) demand for the patented product/method, (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing alternatives (or that the patentee lost sales due to infringement), (3) the patentee had manufacturing and marketing capacity to meet the infringing sales it claims, and (4) the amount of profit the patentee would have made but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If lost profits are not proven for particular infringing sales, the law requires awarding a reasonable royalty for those sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — entitlement and definition (hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lost profits are not proven (or only partially proven), the patent holder is entitled to a reasonable royalty for the infringing sales. A reasonable royalty is the payment that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation between the patent holder and the alleged infringer at the time when the infringing sales began, assuming both parties believed the patent was valid and infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must assume willingness to enter into agreement; assess what a reasonable businessperson would have agreed to. Georgia-Pacific factors and other real-world facts may be considered to determine the royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia‑Pacific factors and other real-world factors for reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered in determining a reasonable royalty include (non-exhaustive): royalties received for licensing the patent, rates paid for comparable patents, nature/scope of the license, patentee's licensing policy, commercial relationship between parties, effect of patented specialty on other sales, alternatives to the patented technology, portion of profit attributable to the invention vs nonpatented elements, duration of patent, established profitability and commercial success, expert testimony, and any other economic factor a prudent businessperson would consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of factors (from Georgia‑Pacific and subsequent cases) provided as illustrative; jury may consider licenses, comparable patents, industry practices, and the significance of the patented technology to the infringer's profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model verdict forms and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample verdict forms (Form A simple; Form B for more complex cases) provide structured questions for the jury on literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents, contributory and inducing infringement, willfulness, various invalidity grounds (obviousness, written description, enablement, best mode, anticipation, inventorship), and damages (lost profits and reasonable royalty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms show question phrasing (Yes/No), where thresholds differ (e.g., 'more probable than not' vs 'highly probable'), and separate entries for damages calculation; courts may tailor forms to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history / file wrapper relevance (prosecution history estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history (communications between applicant and PTO) is part of the public record and can affect claim interpretation and the availability of equivalents (prosecution history estoppel may bar some equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues of prosecution history estoppel are legal questions resolved by a judge rather than the jury; jury should be instructed about limitations on doctrine of equivalents where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions noted by the Committee (indefiniteness and inequitable conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee omitted instructions on indefiniteness (matter for the court) and on inequitable conduct (normally for the court rather than the jury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should provide such instructions only if appropriate; the Committee explains why those topics were not included in model jury instructions.
